pr_body:
Refactored taint_manager tests, namely: removed time.Sleep and simplified main logic. This PR fixes issue(#111140), where there was proposed to remove sleeps from the logic of taint_manager tests. 
Due to made refactoring, tests became faster to run and easier to understand.

/kind feature

> Refactoring of taint manager to inject a fake clock by tests would eliminate the use of sleep and periodic polls

As far as I know, implementing some functionality for test purpose is not a good idea.

> > Refactoring of taint manager to inject a fake clock by tests would eliminate the use of sleep and periodic polls
> 
> As far as I know, implementing some functionality for test purpose is not a good idea.

Yes, but I would not say that extending the class to accept a clock is new functionality. This PR applies this strategy to improve stability of time-based unit tests in job_controller: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/110710. The idea is to replace the time package invocations, such as this one: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d581cc90adba6c84919738841fe3e07302d53e33/pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/scheduler/taint_manager.go#L499, with calls to clock. Then, you can pass a fake clock in unit tests in order to control the time-based behavior of the class.

@mimowo I have completely analyzed your suggestion, and don't agree with it. Even watching at some tests in 'disruption_test.go' we can see, that fake clock does not help in some cases, if wait loops are not used(https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f313ef501a508cedfca9ed5543cdadbb8053c9b9/pkg/controller/disruption/disruption_test.go#L1518-L1522). Having looked at coverage tests, fake clock also does not help so much. That's why I suggest, not to use fake clocks, but just minimize responsibilities of wait loops(not checking actions log, but monitoring node and pod queues, to understand, if we still need to wait or not). I mean, there are some functionality, that can be used with fake clock, but it won't fully help in all cases

Thanks for taking a look at the fake clocks, they indeed do not eliminate every wait, because we often still need to wait for the controller to go through its code. However, fake clocks are useful if the controller enters some code based on the timing (using the clock's functions: Now, Sleep, Since etc.). 

For example the `disruption_test.go` you reference is very useful to see this. This test case tests that the DisruptionTarget condition is removed. However, the controller has its logic to wait for 2min before attempting to delete the DisruptionTarget (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/99360e5dbc26c60c773a9e8b0d2f95960e49e284/pkg/controller/disruption/disruption.go#L77). Thus, if we used the real clock then the test would take at least 2min. The use of a fake clock makes the disruption controller think that the 2min passed already and it should remove the condition. However, we still need to wait for a couple of milliseconds typically, because the code of the controller still needs to execute.

Similarly in the taint_manager, we will not be able to eliminate the waits, but the use of fake clocks would allow us to immediately enter the taint_manager code which is protected by time checks. In particular I was thinking about this test case:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/99360e5dbc26c60c773a9e8b0d2f95960e49e284/pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/scheduler/taint_manager_test.go#L585
In this test case we wait 1s unnecessarily, as expectedDeleteTimes = 1s. Shifting a fake clock by 1s would allow the test to immediately progress with the pod eviction. I think this is the check: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/99360e5dbc26c60c773a9e8b0d2f95960e49e284/pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/scheduler/taint_manager.go#L402

Thus, I think ideally we would use fake clocks in this test. However, I would be also ok to say that this is out of scope for this PR (and ticket it separately) as replacing the time.Sleep with wait.PollImmediately is already an improvement.

issue_context.title: Do not use sleep for unit tests in taint_manager_test.go
issue_context.body:
The taint_manager_test.go uses sleep to wait for some conditions. Example
```
                // TODO(mborsz): Remove this sleep and other sleeps in this file.
		time.Sleep(timeForControllerToProgress)
```

This strategy has at least two problems:
- makes the test longer than needed, because the condition will be met often sooner than the sleep takes
- the test may fail on slower machines or machines under load

Closing as it has been largely addressed by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/113386. In particular the PR addressed the comment mentioned in the issue description. 

The remaining sleeps for sanity testing could be addressed in another dedicated PR. Similarly, performance of the tests can be further improved by fake clock, for example of this test case: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c474920bb1b0af27f2ab9e48160fdafc1523be7f/pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/scheduler/taint_manager_test.go#L285. Still, once needed the improvements will be done under dedicated Issue/PRs.

review_comments:
It seems we might be reducing the test coverage here by not asserting on the delete times.
I suggest using fake.clock to simulate the time passage. For example: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/disruption/disruption_test.go

This will also require modifying the implementation of the taint_manager to use a clock rather than call time directly. For example implementation using a clock check: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/disruption/disruption.go
Oh, ok. Now the coverage is 90%, but, I think it will increase it
Don't you think, that it's better to make a new PR for such task?

I think we should avoid making temporary regressions in coverage. Even if it is not regression in the sense of % it is sort of conceptual regression as we don't assert on the timings. 

Thus, I suggest either:
- revert the unnecessary simplification in this PR and use the fake clock in a followup PR or,
- use a fake clock as part of this PR. 

The use of fake clock would also eliminate the waiting functions used to assert in the other places.
Instead of the if, pass if the delete is expected (maybe actually pass the set of pods for which the delete is expected)
Why two loops, just `for _, action := range client.Actions() {`
Here you return from the function as soon as any of the pod names are encountered. Instead, compute the set of encountered pod names, and compare the entire sets.
